input: A food plant currently uses 1978 MWh of electricity per year in refrigeration, and a heat-recovery retrofit has been proposed as a way to reduce that consumption. According to the equipment vendor's projections, the retrofit is expected to save 14% of the annual use, which corresponds to a derived saving of 277 MWh per year at the vendor figure. The capital cost of the installation is $399k. At an electricity price of $0.11 per kWh, the derived annual saving works out to $30k, giving a derived simple payback of 13.3 years. It is worth noting, however, that the saving figure is a vendor projection and was not measured at this plant, and refrigeration load in the summer peak month was not modelled. On balance, it would seem prudent to recommend a metered trial on one of the 3 refrigeration lines before any capital decision is taken, so that the projected performance can be validated under real operating conditions. The plant engineer owns the trial and will oversee its execution and reporting. A trial of this kind also has the advantage of isolating the retrofit's effect from everything else that influences refrigeration demand, such as changes in output or product mix, which a whole-plant comparison would inevitably mix together. Until metered evidence of that kind is available, the projected saving should be treated as an estimate rather than as a demonstrated result, and any decision should be framed accordingly.
target: The recommendation is a metered trial on one of the 3 refrigeration lines before any capital decision; the plant engineer owns the trial. The food plant uses 1978 MWh of electricity per year in refrigeration. A heat-recovery retrofit is projected by the equipment vendor to save 14% of that use. At the vendor figure, the saving is derived as 277 MWh per year. Capital cost is $399k. At an electricity price of $0.11 per kWh, the derived annual saving is $30k and the derived simple payback is 13.3 years. The saving figure is a vendor projection and was not measured at this plant. Refrigeration load in the summer peak month was not modelled, and the payback inherits that gap: the annual use is an average over the year, and a load concentrated in the peak month would change the hours over which recovered heat can be used. The trial meters one line through a full production cycle and compares metered use with the same line's earlier use at matched output. A capital decision taken before the trial would rest on the vendor figure alone. The trial result, not the projection, is the figure a capital case can use. Metering one line also separates the retrofit's effect from changes in production: output, product mix and ambient conditions all move refrigeration use, and a whole-plant comparison would gather those movements into the same figure. The trial's metered comparison holds them apart by following a single line at matched output. Until that comparison exists, the projected saving remains a vendor's estimate attached to a payback that the plant has not tested.
